old: It traces back to a Greek root meaning 'to be happy,' by way of a word for showing favor.
Its oldest sense was a theological one: a gift or grace freely given.
A German sociologist's use of the word for magnetic leadership got borrowed straight into English — it shares an ancestor with 'charism.'
clues: This personal quality began as a theological term for a gift of grace freely given, from an ancient Greek word linked to one meaning 'to be happy.'
It is the magnetic presence that draws people in and makes them want to follow, something rarer and more compelling than simple charm or likability.
Sociologist Max Weber used it for a leader's special power to inspire devotion; today we say a magnetic politician or rock star simply oozes it.
